twist.stem: Sunil has trained for a year. His cousin has just started. Both do the same 10 push-ups. Is it overload for both of them?
twist.hint: Compare the work with what each one does now.

options.text: For both, since 10 push-ups is the same work.
options.feedback: The count is the same, but overload depends on what each body is used to. For Sunil, 10 push-ups is nothing new.

options.text: Just for the cousin.
options.feedback: Overload means more work than a muscle is used to. Ten push-ups is past the cousin's usual, but it is easy work for Sunil.

options.text: For neither, as push-ups use no added weight.
options.feedback: Body weight can be the load. Ten push-ups is past the cousin's usual work, so it is overload for him.

transfer.stem: Ravi works night shifts as a security guard and has no gym. He wants stronger legs. What can be his load?
transfer.hint: What makes a muscle work past its usual amount?

options.text: No load at all, since he has no weights.
options.feedback: Body weight is a real load, as in push-ups and squats. He can overload his legs with no gym.

options.text: His usual walking rounds, as that is already work.
options.feedback: His rounds are work his legs are used to, so they ask nothing new. Overload means a bit more than usual.

options.text: His own body weight, in squats.
options.feedback: Body weight can be the load. Squats ask his legs for more than they are used to, which is what overload means.

twist.stem: Hari does the same strength routine each week. Which sign tells him it is time to grow the work?
twist.hint: What does it mean when the body has caught up?

options.text: His usual sets feel easy.
options.feedback: Easy work means the body has caught up with it. That is the cue to add a little weight, a few clean reps or a day.

options.text: His legs still ache after each workout.
options.feedback: Soreness is not the cue to add more. When his usual sets feel easy with good form, the body has caught up.

options.text: A month has passed, however the sets feel.
options.feedback: The calendar is not the cue. When the work feels easy with clean form, his body has caught up.

transfer.stem: Preeti is preparing for a state police fitness test at home. She owns no weights and can only train on her three free evenings. Her 20 push-ups now feel easy. What can she change?
transfer.hint: Which of the three levers is still open to her?

options.text: No change until she can buy weights.
options.feedback: Weights are only one way. A few more clean reps also grows the work, using her own body weight.

options.text: Add a few more clean reps.
options.feedback: Work can grow by weight, reps or days. With no weights and no extra days free, a few more clean reps still grows the work.

options.text: Faster, half-depth push-ups to fit more in.
options.feedback: Sloppy half reps are not clean work. A few more full, clean reps is how she grows it.

twist.stem: Deepa ran 150 minutes a week, then took two weeks off for exams. Now she plans to go straight back to 150. How big is that jump next to what she has been doing lately?
twist.hint: Compare it with her last two weeks, not her old best.

options.text: Small, since 150 minutes was her old normal.
options.feedback: Her old normal is not what she does now. After two weeks off, going straight to 150 is a large jump.

options.text: No jump, since the body keeps the old amount.
options.feedback: Jump size compares the new amount with what she does now. Right now that is close to zero, so 150 is big.

options.text: Big, next to almost nothing.
options.feedback: Jump size is judged against what you do now. After two weeks off, 150 minutes is a big rise on almost nothing.

transfer.stem: Riya dances about 40 minutes a week. For her cousin's sangeet in a month, she plans to jump to 200 minutes next week. What fits this step better?
transfer.hint: Compare the rise with what she does now.

options.text: Climb in small steps each week toward it.
options.feedback: A rise that is big next to what you already do is linked to injury. Going from 40 to 200 at once is a huge jump.

options.text: Jump to 200, since dancing is fun, not training.
options.feedback: Fun or not, it is still work for her body. A jump that is big next to her usual 40 is linked to injury.

options.text: Jump to 200, as a big start builds fitness faster.
options.feedback: Bigger jumps are not better. The size of each weekly rise, next to her usual amount, is linked to injury.

twist.stem: Pallavi does squats and push-ups four times a week but eats very little dal, eggs, milk or other protein foods. What is her muscle building short of?
twist.hint: Training is one half of the pair.

options.text: No gap, as training builds the muscle by itself.
options.feedback: Training gives the signal, but the muscle still needs protein from food as its building parts.

options.text: The parts from food that muscle is built from.
options.feedback: Strength work tells a muscle to build, and protein from food gives it the parts. Training alone is half the pair.

options.text: More training days, to make up the gap.
options.feedback: More training adds more signal, not more parts. Protein from food supplies the parts the muscle builds with.

transfer.stem: On a long tour, a Rajkot cricket academy cancels the boys' strength sessions but keeps handing out protein bars. What happens to the bars' protein, for muscle?
transfer.hint: Which half of the pair has been dropped?

options.text: It keeps building muscle, so training can wait.
options.feedback: Protein alone does not build muscle. The body needs the training signal to use it for building.

options.text: It builds even more muscle while the boys rest.
options.feedback: Rest after training helps, but here there is no training. Without the signal, protein is not used for muscle.

options.text: It is not used for muscle.
options.feedback: Strength work is the signal to build. Without it, the body does not use protein to build muscle, however much is eaten.

twist.stem: Babita trains and eats about 1 g of protein per kilo a day. Where does that sit next to the two figures on the card?
twist.hint: Place 1 g between the two numbers.

options.text: Above the need, below the cap.
options.feedback: Healthy adults need 0.83 g per kilo, and gains stopped past about 1.6 g. So 1 g sits between the two.

options.text: Below the basic amount a healthy adult needs.
options.feedback: The basic need is 0.83 g per kilo a day. At 1 g, she is already above it.

options.text: Past the point where extra protein still adds muscle.
options.feedback: Extra protein stopped adding muscle past about 1.6 g per kilo. At 1 g, she is still below that.

transfer.stem: A supplement seller in a Kanpur gym pushes Arif, who weighs 80 kg and trains, to take 200 g of protein a day for faster gains. What does the step show about this?
transfer.hint: Use the higher per-kilo figure for his weight.

options.text: More protein, more muscle, so 200 g beats 128 g.
options.feedback: Muscle can use only so much. Past about 1.6 g per kilo, or 128 g for him, extra added no more muscle.

options.text: Past about 128 g, extra protein added no more muscle.
options.feedback: In strength training, more than about 1.6 g per kilo a day added no more muscle. For 80 kg that is about 128 g.

options.text: It is too little, as he needs 1.6 g per gram of muscle.
options.feedback: The figure is 1.6 g per kilo of body weight, not per gram of muscle. For him that is about 128 g.

twist.stem: Ishita, 20, and her father, 55, do the same strength session. How does the rise in muscle building tend to compare?
twist.hint: The research found a difference with age.

options.text: It tends to be the same, as the session matched.
options.feedback: The same session can bring a different rise. In adults over 50, the rise in muscle building was smaller.

options.text: Bigger, since he has more to rebuild.
options.feedback: The rise was smaller in adults over 50, not bigger. Age changed how much the building process rose.

options.text: His rise is smaller.
options.feedback: After a session, muscle building can stay raised for up to two days. In adults over 50, the rise was smaller.

transfer.stem: Kiran plays a hard kabaddi match on Saturday evening. On Sunday she sits at her desk all day studying. What may be going on in her muscles on Sunday?
transfer.hint: How long can the process stay on after a session?

options.text: Building is still switched on.
options.feedback: After hard muscle work, the building process can stay switched on for up to two days. Her rest day is part of it.

options.text: No building, since growth happens during the match.
options.feedback: Building does not stop when the match ends. It can stay raised for up to two days after.

options.text: Building waits until her soreness has faded away.
options.feedback: Building does not wait for soreness to end. It can stay raised for up to two days right after the work.

twist.stem: Which of these nights falls inside the adult range?
twist.hint: Count the hours in each, then compare.

options.text: 12:30 am to 6 am.
options.feedback: That is only five and a half hours. Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours a night.

options.text: 11 pm to 7 am.
options.feedback: That is 8 hours, inside the 7 to 9 hours advised for adults. The other two nights fall short of 7.

options.text: 2 am to 8:30 am.
options.feedback: That is six and a half hours, which is still under 7. Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours a night.

transfer.stem: In harvest season, a farmer in Haryana works long days in the fields and sleeps about 5 hours a night. What do the short nights cut into?
transfer.hint: When does much of the mending happen?

options.text: No real repair, since that matters for athletes.
options.feedback: Repair in sleep happens for every adult, not just athletes. Short nights cut into it.

options.text: Just his energy, not any repair.
options.feedback: Sleep is more than a break. Deep sleep helps build muscle and repair tissue, so short nights cut repair too.

options.text: Time his body uses to fix tissue in deep sleep.
options.feedback: Deep sleep releases a hormone that helps build muscle and repair tissue. Short nights cut into that time.

twist.stem: Before a district final, Neeraj sleeps badly for just one night. Does a single short night matter, by the review of athletes?
twist.hint: How much sleep loss did the studies look at?

options.text: Yes, even one night lowered play.
options.feedback: In the review, short-term sleep loss, often a single night, lowered sports performance.

options.text: No, it takes weeks of short sleep before play drops.
options.feedback: The review looked at short-term loss, often one night, and it still tended to lower play.

options.text: No, match nerves tend to keep him just as sharp.
options.feedback: Nerves did not cancel it out. Even one short night tended to lower play in the review.

transfer.stem: Sports day is the morning after a family wedding. Plan A: leave the wedding at 2 am and wake at the usual 8. Plan B: sleep at the usual 10 but wake at 4 to drive back. Which tends to hurt play less?
transfer.hint: Look at which end of sleep each choice cuts.

options.text: Waking at 4, since the bedtime stays normal.
options.feedback: A normal bedtime does not save it. Losing the end of the night hurt sport most in the review.

options.text: Leaving late and waking at the usual time.
options.feedback: In the review, losing the end of the night hurt sport most, and losing the start showed no clear drop.

options.text: Both the same, as each loses sleep.
options.feedback: Both lose sleep, but not the same part. Losing the end of the night hurt sport more than losing the start.

twist.stem: After a short night, which way do the two hunger hormones move?
twist.hint: One makes you hungry; the other helps you feel full.

options.text: Ghrelin down, leptin up.
options.feedback: That is the reverse. Short sleep raises the hunger hormone ghrelin and lowers the fullness hormone leptin.

options.text: Both go up together.
options.feedback: They move in opposite ways. Ghrelin goes up and leptin goes down, so you feel hungrier.

options.text: Ghrelin up, leptin down.
options.feedback: Short sleep raises ghrelin, which makes you hungry, and lowers leptin, which helps you feel full.

transfer.stem: After a week of late nights to meet office deadlines, Varun keeps snacking at his desk, though his work is no harder than usual. Which cause fits this step?
transfer.hint: What did the late nights do inside his body?

options.text: Short sleep shifts hunger hormones.
options.feedback: Short sleep raises ghrelin, the hunger hormone, and lowers leptin, the fullness hormone. So he feels hungrier.

options.text: His brain burns far more food when he works late.
options.feedback: His work is no harder than usual. Short sleep shifts his hunger hormones, which makes him want more food.

options.text: It is just boredom; sleep plays no part.
options.feedback: Sleep plays a part. Too little of it raises the hunger hormone and lowers the fullness hormone.

twist.stem: In Nagpur in May, a cricket camp can train at 6 am, 1 pm or 7 pm. Which plan fits the hot-weather plan best?
twist.hint: Think about the clock and the pace.

options.text: 1 pm, at a hard pace, to build heat toughness.
options.feedback: Heat adds strain; it is not a bonus workout. Cooler hours and a slow start are the safer plan.

options.text: 6 am or 7 pm, with an easy start.
options.feedback: Hot days call for cooler hours and a slow start. Early morning or evening, eased into, fits both parts.

options.text: 1 pm, but with a slow start.
options.feedback: A slow start helps, but 1 pm is the hottest choice. The plan also moves training to cooler hours.

transfer.stem: A building site foreman in Ahmedabad plans the heaviest lifting for a heatwave week. When does that work fit best?
transfer.hint: The body has to shed heat as well as work.

options.text: Midday, to finish fast while workers are fresh.
options.feedback: Midday is the hottest time, so the same work is harder. Cooler hours and a slow start fit better.

options.text: Any time, if the work is done quickly.
options.feedback: Rushing does not help in heat. Cooler hours and a slow start make the same work easier on the body.

options.text: Early in the day, with a slow start.
options.feedback: In heat, the body works to shed heat as well as move. Cooler hours and a slow start make the same work easier.

twist.stem: After a hot match, Kunal is not thirsty, but he forces down two litres at once to catch up. What is the problem?
twist.hint: Does more always mean safer here?

options.text: Forcing water when not thirsty raises risk.
options.feedback: Sipping through the session suits hot days. Forcing water on someone who is not thirsty raises risk.

options.text: None, since more water is the safer choice.
options.feedback: More is not always safer. Forcing water when not thirsty raises risk, so sipping through the session is better.

options.text: He needed salt water instead of food.
options.feedback: Food is the easiest way to put salt back. The problem here is forcing water when he is not thirsty.

transfer.stem: On a long summer pilgrimage walk to Pandharpur, Ganesh sweats a lot all day. What is the easiest way to put back the salt he loses?
transfer.hint: Sweat takes more than water out.

options.text: No need, since water alone puts the salt back.
options.feedback: Water does not hold the salt that left in sweat. Salty food is the easiest way to replace it.

options.text: With his meals and salty snacks.
options.feedback: Sweat takes salt as well as water. Food is the easiest way to put the salt back.

options.text: By gulping big amounts of water at each stop.
options.feedback: Forcing down big amounts raises risk, and water does not bring salt back. Food does that most easily.

twist.stem: Neha felt sick in the heat, so she stopped and rested in the shade. Then she throws up. What now?
twist.hint: Which signs mean more than rest is needed?

options.text: Wait an hour to see if it passes.
options.feedback: Vomiting is a sign not to wait. Heat illness can get worse, so get medical help.

options.text: Drink a lot of water fast, then carry on.
options.feedback: Gulping water and carrying on is not the step. Throwing up in the heat calls for medical help.

options.text: Get medical help.
options.feedback: Stopping, cooling and sipping water come first. Throwing up is a sign to get medical help.

transfer.stem: At a summer baraat in Jaipur, Kavita's uncle dances in the sun for an hour. Then he feels dizzy and gets a headache. What is the safe move?
transfer.hint: Think about what these signs mean in the heat.

options.text: Stop dancing, move into shade, and sip water.
options.feedback: Dizziness or headache in the heat mean stop, get cool and sip water, because heat illness can get worse.

options.text: Keep dancing; it will pass once he sweats more.
options.feedback: These are warning signs, not something to push through. He needs to stop, get cool and sip water.

options.text: Gulp a big cold drink and carry on.
options.feedback: A drink alone, then carrying on, misses the step. Signs like these mean stop and get somewhere cool.

twist.stem: After a hard run, which finish fits a cool-down?
twist.hint: A cool-down is the warm-up's idea, at the other end.

options.text: Stopping dead and sitting down at once.
options.feedback: Stopping at once skips the easing down. A cool-down is the same activity done slower, then lighter.

options.text: Easy jogging, then walking.
options.feedback: A cool-down is the activity done slower or lighter, so heart rate and breathing come down bit by bit.

options.text: A last flat-out sprint to finish strong.
options.feedback: A sprint raises effort, which is the opposite of cooling down. Easy jogging, then walking, brings it down.

transfer.stem: Before a Navratri garba night in Vadodara, which start fits a warm-up best?
transfer.hint: Same move, lighter effort.

options.text: Long toe-touch holds, then straight into fast steps.
options.feedback: A warm-up is mainly the activity done easier, not long holds. Slow rounds of the steps fit better.

options.text: Full speed from the start, to heat up quickly.
options.feedback: A warm-up starts easy, not at full effort. Slow rounds let heart rate and breathing rise bit by bit.

options.text: A few slow rounds of the garba steps first.
options.feedback: A warm-up is the activity done slower or lighter, so heart rate and breathing climb bit by bit.

twist.stem: Before a jump test, one group holds each stretch for 90 seconds and another for 20 seconds. How did the average drops compare in the review?
twist.hint: Find which side of the line each group sits on.

options.text: The long holds cost about four times as much.
options.feedback: Holds of 60 seconds or more cut results by about 4.6%, against about 1.1% for shorter holds. That is about four times as much.

options.text: The short holds cost more, as they feel rushed.
options.feedback: It is the other way round. Long holds of 60 seconds or more cost about 4.6%, short ones about 1.1%.

options.text: About the same, since any still hold costs the same.
options.feedback: Hold length matters. Shorter holds cut results by only about 1.1%, against about 4.6% for long ones.

transfer.stem: Before her Kathak audition, which has fast jumps, Rhea holds each leg stretch for 90 seconds, then waits still for her turn. Which change fits the review?
transfer.hint: Find what made the drop disappear.

options.text: Hold each stretch even longer, to loosen fully.
options.feedback: Longer holds cost more, not less. Holds of 60 seconds or more cut results by about 4.6%.

options.text: Shorter holds, or active moves after them.
options.feedback: Long still holds cut jump results soon after. Shorter holds cost much less, and with active moves after, no clear effect was seen.

options.text: Stretch harder, then rest still until her turn.
options.feedback: Resting still after long holds is what was linked to the drop. Active moves after the stretch showed no clear effect.

twist.stem: A coach reads that stretching showed no clear effect on injuries. He decides to drop stretching from warm-ups. What does the review still suggest?
twist.hint: Look at what comes after the stretches.

options.text: Drop it, since it does not cut injuries.
options.feedback: No clear injury effect is not the whole story. The review still suggests stretching inside a warm-up ending in active moves.

options.text: Make it the whole warm-up, since it stops injuries.
options.feedback: Stretching had no clear effect on injuries. It fits inside a warm-up that ends with active moves.

options.text: Keep it, followed by active moves.
options.feedback: Stretching showed no clear effect on injuries, but the review still suggests it inside a warm-up that ends with active moves.

transfer.stem: A courier in Mumbai stretches at 8 am before his rounds, sure it will keep him free of strains all day. What does the evidence show?
transfer.hint: Think about how long extra reach lasts.

options.text: Gains fade fast, and injuries showed no clear drop.
options.feedback: Range gains from stretching usually last under 30 minutes. A big review also found no clear effect on overall injuries.

options.text: He is right; a morning stretch protects him until night.
options.feedback: Range gains usually fade within 30 minutes, and stretching showed no clear effect on injuries.

options.text: It works if he holds each stretch for two minutes.
options.feedback: Longer holds do not make the gain last all day. Range gains usually fade within 30 minutes.

twist.stem: On a walk, Aditi can easily sing a full song. What effort is that?
twist.hint: Where does easy singing sit on the voice test?

options.text: Moderate, since she is out walking.
options.feedback: Moderate is when you can talk but not sing. Singing easily means her effort is lighter than that.

options.text: Lighter than moderate.
options.feedback: Talk but not sing marks moderate effort. If she can sing easily, she is working below that.

options.text: Vigorous, since singing takes breath.
options.feedback: At vigorous effort only a few words fit before a breath. Singing a full song is lighter than moderate.

transfer.stem: A postman in Kerala cycles his rounds. He can chat with shopkeepers as he rides, but he cannot sing along to the radio. What effort is that?
transfer.hint: Check what his voice can and cannot do.

options.text: Too easy to count, since he can chat.
options.feedback: Being able to talk does not mean too easy. Talk but no singing marks moderate effort.

options.text: Vigorous, as he works for hours.
options.feedback: A long day is not the test. At vigorous effort he could only say a few words before a breath.

options.text: Moderate.
options.feedback: Talk but not sing marks moderate effort. Vigorous would leave him only a few words before a breath.

twist.stem: Raj rates his brisk walk a 6 today. After months of regular walks at the same speed, what might he rate it?
twist.hint: Fitness changes how hard a task feels.

options.text: Lower, as fitter people need less effort.
options.feedback: Effort is personal. As he gets fitter, the same walk takes less effort, so his rating can drop.

options.text: Still 6, since the walk is the same.
options.feedback: The walk is the same, but his fitness is not. Fitter people need less effort for the same activity.

options.text: Higher, as tired muscles build up over months.
options.feedback: Regular walking makes him fitter, not more tired. The same walk then takes less effort.

transfer.stem: During Diwali cleaning, Asha scrubs the floors and rates the effort an 8 on the 0 to 10 scale. Which band is that?
transfer.hint: Find where the top band begins.

options.text: Moderate, since it is just housework.
options.feedback: The scale rates effort, not the kind of task. An 8 is in the vigorous band, whatever the activity.

options.text: Vigorous.
options.feedback: On the 0 to 10 scale, moderate is 5 or 6, and vigorous starts at 7 or 8. So an 8 is vigorous.

options.text: Too light to count, since it is not exercise.
options.feedback: Any activity can be rated by effort. An 8 marks vigorous effort on the scale.

twist.stem: After a month back, Kavya's brisk 20-minute walks feel easy. What is the next step in the build-up order?
twist.hint: Which comes first: time or intensity?

options.text: Switch to fast running right away.
options.feedback: That raises effort first. The order is minutes and days first, then effort later.

options.text: Keep it the same, since any change risks injury.
options.feedback: Small additions are part of the plan. Add minutes and days first, then effort.

options.text: Walk a few more minutes, or one more day.
options.feedback: After time off, add minutes and days first, and effort later. Running can come after that.

transfer.stem: After two years with no exercise, Meher joins a bhangra class where others dance flat out. Which plan fits her first weeks?
transfer.hint: Use her voice as a guide to effort.

options.text: A pace she can talk through.
options.feedback: After time off, start at a moderate effort you can talk through. Add minutes and days first, effort later.

options.text: Match the others' full effort so she can catch up quickly.
options.feedback: Starting hard to catch up is the risky choice. After time off, start moderate and build up.

options.text: Hard bursts with long rests, since short efforts are safe.
options.feedback: Short does not make hard effort the right start. After time off, begin at a moderate effort.

twist.stem: After work, Mohan can only manage a slow stroll, not a brisk walk. Is it worth it?
twist.hint: Compare it with doing nothing on the sofa.

options.text: No, as just brisk bouts give any gain.
options.feedback: Brisk bouts count toward the weekly total, but a stroll still beats sitting. Some activity is better than none.

options.text: Yes, some movement beats sitting.
options.feedback: Some activity is better than none. Brisk bouts count toward the total, and a stroll is still better than sitting.

options.text: Yes, but just if it lasts 10 minutes or more.
options.feedback: The 10-minute rule was dropped. Any movement, short or long, is better than sitting.

transfer.stem: Ankur works in a Pune office. Several times a day, he takes the stairs to the third floor briskly instead of the lift. A colleague thinks it is too short to matter. Does it count?
transfer.hint: Was the old time rule kept or dropped?

options.text: It counts if each climb lasts 10 minutes.
options.feedback: The 10-minute minimum was dropped. Brisk bouts of any length count.

options.text: No, as planned workouts are what count.
options.feedback: Brisk stairs and walks count too. Some activity is better than none, and short bouts add up.

options.text: Yes, brisk bouts of any length add up.
options.feedback: The old 10-minute rule was dropped, so brisk bouts of any length count. Even a few flights of stairs counts.

twist.stem: Neha does her push-ups at random times: some days at dawn, some at night. After two months they still feel like a chore to start. What is the likely reason?
twist.hint: What starts a habit running on its own?

options.text: No steady cue sets them off.
options.feedback: A habit forms when one small thing is done at the same time each day. Random times leave no cue to set it off.

options.text: Two months is far too short for any habit.
options.feedback: Time alone is not the issue. Without a steady daily cue, the push-ups never start to run on their own.

options.text: Push-ups are too hard to become a habit.
options.feedback: The move is not the problem. Tied to the same daily cue, a small action can become a habit.

transfer.stem: Ishaan wants a daily habit of reading a few pages of a novel. Which plan fits this step best?
transfer.hint: Look for a small step tied to something daily.

options.text: A whole chapter whenever he has free time.
options.feedback: Free time comes at random, so there is no steady cue. A small step after a daily event works better.

options.text: Two pages right after his evening chai.
options.feedback: One small action at the same time each day starts to run on its own, because the cue sets it off.

options.text: A big goal: twenty books by the end of the year.
options.feedback: A goal is not a cue. A small action tied to a daily event is what turns into a habit.

twist.stem: Pooja's habit plan is a 45-minute run each day. She misses one day and feels like giving up. What does the study point to instead?
twist.hint: Think about how big each day's task is.

options.text: Make up the missed day with a double run tomorrow.
options.feedback: A miss does not need making up. Gains soon pick up again, and a small step keeps restarts easy.

options.text: Start the count again from day one, fresh.
options.feedback: One miss did not seriously harm habit forming. There is no need to restart; a smaller step helps.

options.text: A smaller daily step.
options.feedback: Missing the odd day did not seriously harm habits. Small, easy changes help, because an early setback can be discouraging.

transfer.stem: Each night, Kabir writes down what he spent that day. He skips one night because of a cousin's wedding. What happens to the habit?
transfer.hint: Did one miss do serious harm in the study?

options.text: It carries on if he writes again the next night.
options.feedback: Missing the odd day did not seriously harm habit forming, and gains soon picked up again.

options.text: It is broken, so he has to restart the count.
options.feedback: One missed day did not seriously harm habit forming. Going back the next night keeps it going.

options.text: It carries on, as long as he makes up the missed night.
options.feedback: No catching up is needed. Simply going back to the usual small step the next night keeps the habit going.

twist.stem: A label lists 14 g added sugars and 8 g total sugars. What is wrong with it?
twist.hint: Which line holds the other one?

options.text: It is fine, since added sugar is extra on top.
options.feedback: Added sugars are part of total sugars, not extra. So added cannot be more than the total.

options.text: Added sugars cannot be more than the total.
options.feedback: Total sugars count every sugar, added ones included. So the added line can never be bigger than the total.

options.text: The food's own sugar must be 22 g.
options.feedback: That adds the two lines, but added is already inside the total. A larger added line is an error.

transfer.stem: Choosing a breakfast cereal for her hostel room, Lata compares two packs. Pack A: 10 g total sugars, 0 g added. Pack B: 8 g total sugars, 8 g added. Which has more sugar put in?
transfer.hint: Which line counts just what was put in?

options.text: Pack A, since its total sugars line is higher.
options.feedback: Total counts every sugar, including the food's own. Pack A has 0 g added, so Pack B has more put in.

options.text: Both the same, since each pack has sugar in it.
options.feedback: The added lines differ: 0 g against 8 g. Pack B has more sugar put in.

options.text: Pack B, with 8 g added.
options.feedback: Added sugars are only the ones put in. Pack A's sugar is the food's own, while all of Pack B's was added.

twist.stem: A plain noodle pack shows a photo of noodles topped with vegetables and prawns, marked 'serving suggestion'. Must the label give a % of prawns?
twist.hint: Not every image on a pack counts.

options.text: No, serving suggestions are left out.
options.feedback: A stressed ingredient usually needs its %, but serving-suggestion pictures are left out of the rule.

options.text: Yes, any food shown in a picture needs a %.
options.feedback: Not every picture counts. Serving-suggestion pictures are left out, as are spices used for flavour.

options.text: Yes, but just for the vegetables, not prawns.
options.feedback: The vegetables and prawns are both part of the serving suggestion, which is left out of the rule.

transfer.stem: Buying breakfast at a Chennai supermarket, Suresh picks a masala oats pack. The front stresses 'with real almonds' and shows turmeric and pepper. Which needs a % on the label?
transfer.hint: Flavourings are a special case.

options.text: The almonds, turmeric and pepper, since each is shown.
options.feedback: Spices used for flavour are left out of the rule. Only the stressed almonds need a %.

options.text: The almonds, but not the spices.
options.feedback: A stressed ingredient must usually show its %, but spices used for flavour are left out of the rule.

options.text: None, since oats are the main ingredient.
options.feedback: Stressing an ingredient in words or pictures brings the % rule in. The almonds need a %.

twist.stem: A serving's label shows 40% next to added sugars. About how many grams of added sugar is that serving?
twist.hint: Take that share of the reference day's amount.

options.text: About 40 g.
options.feedback: The % is a share of 50 g, not a gram count. 40% of 50 g is about 20 g.

options.text: About 25 g.
options.feedback: The % compares with a 50 g reference day. 40% of 50 g is 20 g, not 25 g.

options.text: About 20 g.
options.feedback: The reference day counts 50 g of added sugar. 40% of 50 g is 20 g.

transfer.stem: A masala chai premix lists 10 g added sugar per sachet. Dadi drinks three cups a day, one sachet each. About what share of the reference day's added sugar is that?
transfer.hint: Find one cup's share, then count the cups.

options.text: About 60%.
options.feedback: One sachet's 10 g is 20% of the 50 g reference. Three cups make about 60%.

options.text: About 20%, as the label shows.
options.feedback: The %RDA is per serving. Three servings make three times that, so about 60%.

options.text: About 30%.
options.feedback: Each 10 g sachet is 20% of the 50 g reference. Three of them make about 60%.
